info.bio:
The Searchers constituye uno de los principales grupos cultores del llamado Liverpool Sound.  Su principal característica es la de poseer un ritmo muy fuerte ya que prácticamente presentan 2 guitarras rítmicas; pocos son los temas en los que podemos apreciar un solo.  Las guitarras, especialmente en sus primeros discos, están sobriamente acompañadas por una batería igualmente impactante.

Su primer álbum para el sello PYE presenta temas como "Love Potion Number Nine"

scenes.name: Pop protesta y folk rock (1965)
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El pop quería profundidad y el folk quería fama. En 1963 Dylan condensó el miedo atómico en «A Hard Rain’s a-Gonna Fall» y Peter, Paul and Mary llevaron «Blowin’ in the Wind» al número 2; en 1964 los Searchers demostraron que una letra sobre lluvia radiactiva («What Have They Done to the Rain») podía entrar en el Top 20. En 1965 Dylan triunfó en Inglaterra, Donovan arrasó con «Catch the Wind» y el «Mr Tambourine Man» de los Byrds abrió la veda: todos versionaban a Dylan y la «Pop Protest» amenazaba con ser una moda. «Eve of Destruction», de P. F. Sloan cantada por Barry McGuire y prohibida por la BBC, fue su cénit comercial y su nadir artístico. Tom Wilson, productor despedido por Dylan, añadió instrumentos eléctricos a la versión acústica de «The Sound of Silence» de Simon & Garfunkel, primer número 1 estadounidense de 1966 y señal de que el mercado de masas no temería la profundidad.

scenes.name: Beat, R&B y mod pop británico
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Tras el éxito de los Beatles, las cuatro grandes discográficas (EMI, Decca, Pye y Philips) saquearon metódicamente las provincias: firmaban barato y esperaban a ver qué pegaba. Pye, del veterano Louis Benjamin, tenía a los Kinks y a los Searchers y fama de contratos miserables. Los Ugly’s de Birmingham, nacidos del skiffle y curtidos en los clubes alemanes, se distinguían por su conciencia social; la cara B de su tercer single, «A Quiet Explosion» (21 de enero de 1966), con órgano Vox Continental, un riff con eco a lo Delia Derbyshire y un bajo descendente que es la bomba cayendo, desapareció en la sobreproducción del momento, pero es un disco extraño y auténtico que se acerca a la psicodelia. A principios de 1966 las bases del beat y del R&B se llevaron al límite, como bajo una enorme presión: «Keep on Running» de Spencer Davis casa soul y mod pop, los Wheels de Belfast aceleran sin freno en «Bad Little Woman» y los Poets de Glasgow, de Andrew Loog Oldham, desquician el «Baby Don’t You Do It» de Marvin Gaye.

podcast.title: Mike Pender's MBE (2020)
podcast.body: Mike Pender was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire (MBE) in 2020 for his services to the music industry. "Mike Pender was made an MBE in 2020, as a reward for his services to the music industry."

podcast.title: "Farmer John" Becoming a Garage Rock Standard
podcast.body: The Searchers' cover of Dillon Di's "Farmer John" is credited with making it a garage rock standard, as it was not widely known before their version. "Farmer John by Dillon Dui, which hadn't yet become a garage rock standard, and indeed seems to have become so largely because of the searches version."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: A&R Club Demo Session
podcast.body: Lacking talent scout interest, the band recorded a full, short demo album at the A&R Club, where they regularly played, sending it to A&R people. This session captured their "stompiest and hardest driving" sound, which was more powerful than their later studio recordings. "That demo session produced a full, short album, which shows them at their stompiest and hardest driving."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Band Name Origin
podcast.body: The Liverpool band The Searchers, who later became highly influential, took their name from the John Wayne film "The Searchers," which had also inspired Buddy Holly's first version of "That'll Be the Day." "a film which later gave its name to a band from Liverpool who would become hugely influential."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Brian Epstein's Missed Management Opportunity
podcast.body: The Searchers struggled to gain attention from the London music industry partly due to an unfortunate incident where Brian Epstein came to see them, but Tony Jackson was drunk, fell off the stage, and Epstein decided against managing them. "The day that Brian Epstein turned up to see them, with the thoughts of maybe managing them. Tony Jackson was drunk and fell off the stage, and Epstein decided that he would be going to give them a miss."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Chris Curtis as Frontman and Second Lead Singer
podcast.body: After Johnny Sandin's departure, Chris Curtis moved his drum kit to the front of the stage, played standing up, and became the group's frontman and second lead singer, a distinctive move for the band. "In a move which made them stand out, Chris Curtis moved his drum kit to the front line, started playing standing up, and became the group's frontman and second lead singer."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Chris Curtis's Bass Pedal Squeak on "Needles and Pins" Single
podcast.body: The original single mix of "Needles and Pins" is marred by an "incredibly squeaky bass pedal" on Chris Curtis's drum kit. While barely audible on early 60s equipment, modern digital copies make it overpower the music, leading to modified versions on compilations. "The mix used for the original single version of the song, which is what I'm exerting here, is marred by an incredibly squeaky bass pedal on Chris Curtis's drum kit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Chris Curtis's Erratic Behavior and Departure
podcast.body: The other band members grew annoyed with Chris Curtis's song choices and increasingly erratic behavior. During an Australian tour, they flushed his supply of "uppers and downers" down the toilet, leading to his departure from the group upon returning to the UK. "Eventually, on an Australian tour, they took his supply of uppers and downers, which he had been using as much to self-medicators for enjoyment as far as I can tell, and flushed them down the toilet."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Chris Curtis's Post-Searchers Career - Roundabout and Deep Purple Connection
podcast.body: After leaving The Searchers, Chris Curtis released one solo single, "Aggravation," featuring Jimmy Page, John Paul Jones, and Joe Moretti, but it failed to chart. He then formed a band called Roundabout with a rotating lineup concept. However, John Lord and Richie Blackmore, who were part of Roundabout, decided to form Deep Purple after Curtis's departure. "The guitarist and keyboard player quickly decided that it would be more convenient for them if Curtis was the one to hop off, and without Curtis, John Mord and Richie Blackmore went on to form Deep Purple."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Chris Curtis's Sexuality Speculation
podcast.body: Tony Jackson publicly alleged that Chris Curtis was gay and wanted to bring his boyfriend, Frank Allen, into the band. While Allen denied a relationship, Curtis was widely described as gay or bi by contemporaries but never came out publicly, possibly due to strong religious views. There were suggestions Jackson blackmailed the band about Curtis's sexuality for more lead vocals. "There's some suggestion, indeed, that one reason Jackson ended up out of the band was that he blackmailed the band, saying that he would publicly out-curtis if he didn't get more lead vocals."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Clean Living Image vs. Members' Vices
podcast.body: The Searchers were known as the most clean-living Liverpool band, all devout Catholics attending mass weekly and generally avoiding vices common among rock stars. However, Tony Jackson was a heavy drinker who became aggressive when drunk, and Chris Curtis was known for his eccentricity and possible mental illness. "The searches were the most clean living of the Liverpool bands. They were all devout Catholics who would go to mass every Sunday without fail, and seemed to have never indulged in most of the vices that pretty much every other rock star indulged in."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Connection to The Undertakers and Jackie Lomax
podcast.body: As part of their Pye Records deal, The Searchers' manager insisted that Tony Hatch also sign The Undertakers. Although The Undertakers released several flop singles, their lead singer, Jackie Lomax, later released the solo single "Sour Milk Sea," written for him by George Harrison. "The biggest mark that the undertakers would make on music would come many years later, when their lead singer Jackie Lomax would release a solo single, SourMLC, which George Harrison wrote for him."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Controversial Lyric in "Love Potion Number 9"
podcast.body: The lyric for "Love Potion Number 9" contains a word for Romany people that many regard as a slur. "The lyric contains a word for Romany people, which many of those people regard as a slur."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Early Origins Dispute
podcast.body: The story of The Searchers' early origins is highly disputed, with the two surviving original members, John McNally and Mike Pender, having legal disputes and not speaking for 36 years. "As a result, literally everything about the group's history has become a battlefield in their ongoing arguments."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Enduring Influence of Combined Guitar Sound
podcast.body: The jangly 12-string electric guitar sound, originally created by Mike Pender and John McNally playing in unison, proved to be greater than its individual parts and is a lasting legacy. "But every time you hear a jangly 12-string electric guitar, you're hearing a sound that was originally created by Mike Pender and John McNally playing in unison, a sound that proved to be greater than any of its constituent parts."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Financial Struggles and Internal Strife (1980s)
podcast.body: By 1985, The Searchers were at a breaking point due to lack of new material and intense animosity between Mike Pender and John McNally, the only two Liverpool-based members. They were so poor they shared one car for gigs, leading to unpleasant long drives. "The group was so poor that McNally and Pender had one car between the two of them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Internal Conflicts and Factions (Early Days)
podcast.body: Cracks appeared early in the group. Curtis and Jackson didn't get along, and Jackson drifted apart from Pender, leading to a dynamic of "three plus one outsider" by their first recording sessions, with Jackson isolated. "By the time of their first recording sessions, they appeared to most people to be a group of three plus one outsider, with Jackson not getting on well with any of the others."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Invention of Jangle Pop and Folk Rock with "Needles and Pins"
podcast.body: The Searchers' arrangement of "Needles and Pins," by emphasizing the riff with two electric guitars played simultaneously with reverb (creating an electric 12-string sound), inadvertently invented the genres of Jangle Pop and Folk Rock. "That record is the root of Django Pop and Folk Rock."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Jackie DeShannon's Uncredited Co-Authorship of "Needles and Pins"
podcast.body: Jackie DeShannon insists she co-wrote "Needles and Pins" with Sonny Bono and Jack Nitzsche, but her name was left off the credit, likely due to their alleged abusive and misogynistic nature. "Bano and Nitchie are the credited writers on Needles and pins, but Jackie Dishanan insists that she co-wrote the song with them, but her name was left off the credit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: John Lennon's Endorsement of "Sweets For My Sweet"
podcast.body: John Lennon publicly declared "Sweets For My Sweet" the "best record to come out of Liverpool," significantly boosting The Searchers' standing among local groups. "That went to number 1, helped by an endorsement from John Lennon, who said it was the best record to come out of Liverpool, and launched the searches into the very top tier of Liverpool groups."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Johnny Sandin's Departure
podcast.body: Billy Beck, performing as Johnny Sandin, was the lead singer for two years before quitting to join The VMO4, a group managed by Brian Epstein. This left The Searchers without a frontman, leading them to split lead vocals. "The group performed as Johnny Sandin in the searches for two years, before Sandin quit the group to join the VMO4, a group that was managed by Brian Epstein."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Legal Disputes Over Band Name and Touring Rights
podcast.body: Following Mike Pender's departure, extensive litigation ensued between "Mike Pender's Searchers" and the remaining "The Searchers" (with John McNally and Frank Allen). These disputes over billing and naming rights were highly contentious, nearly leading to Pender's imprisonment and threatening both groups with bankruptcy due to undercutting. "A big chunk of the autobiographies of both Pender and Alan are taken up with the ensuing litigation, as there were suits and counter suits over a matter of billing which on the outside look incredibly trivial, but which of course mattered greatly to everyone involved."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Longevity of Rival Bands
podcast.body: Mike Pender continued to tour, and the McNally and Allen lineup performed regularly until 2019, ceasing due to McNally's ill health. Pender's show was noted as being better, sticking to a guitar-based sound, while McNally and Allen's lineup relied on a "cheesy sounding synthesiser." "McNally and Alan's lineup of the group relied rather too heavily on a rather cheesy sounding synthesiser for my taste, while Pender stuck closer to a straight guitar-based drum sound, but both kept audiences very happy for decades."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Mike Pender's Departure and Formation of "Mike Pender's Searchers"
podcast.body: Mike Pender, feeling he was the band's star and resented splitting money three ways (drummers were salaried), decided to tour independently. An agreement was reached for him to tour as "Mike Pender's Searchers," provided all promotional material used equal-sized lettering. "Pender decided that he could make more money by touring at his own, but still doing essentially the same show, with hired backing musicians."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Musical Taste Differences as Creative Drive
podcast.body: A split in musical taste defined much of their creativity: Pender and McNally favored softer country and rockabilly (Everly Brothers, Buddy Holly), while Jackson preferred harder, stomping music. Chris Curtis, however, primarily shaped the group's repertoire, seeking out obscure R&B B-sides and folk music. "There was also a split in the band's musical taste, but that would be the split that would drive much of their creativity."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Name Origin Dispute - "The Searchers"
podcast.body: While everyone agrees the name came from the John Wayne film *The Searchers* (which also inspired Buddy Holly's "That'll Be the Day"), Pender claims it was his idea, while McNally attributes it to an early singer named Big Run. "Pender claims that it was his idea while McNally says that the name was coined by a singer named Big Run, who sang with the band for a bit before disappearing into obscurity."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Posthumous Reconciliation and Enduring Animosity
podcast.body: Tony Jackson and Chris Curtis both died in the 2000s, with Pender and Allen exchanging pleasantries at their funerals. However, John McNally and Mike Pender never reconciled, refusing to speak even after McNally's band retired, with the remaining Searchers' website still prominently asserting ownership of the band name. "McNally and Pender wouldn't even say hello to each other, and even though McNally and Alan's band has retired, there's still a prominent notice on their website that they own the name of the surges, and nobody else is allowed to use it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Pye Records Contract and Tony Hatch
podcast.body: Tony Hatch, a successful songwriter and producer, was impressed by The Searchers' demo and offered to sign them. Their manager agreed on the condition that Hatch also sign The Undertakers, which he did. "Hatch heard the group's demo and was impressed and offered to sign them. The search has managed at the time agreed on one condition that Hatch also signed another band he managed, the undertakers."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Shared Label with The Kinks
podcast.body: The Searchers were signed to Pye Records, which became the label for The Kinks after they were rejected by Decca, EMI, and Philips. This meant The Kinks shared a record label home with The Searchers. "which when the bid default ended up recording for Pie records, the same label as the searchers."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 119: "You Really Got Me" by the Kinks

podcast.title: Sire Records Deal and Revival Attempt
podcast.body: In 1979, Seymour Stein of Sire Records, inspired by The Ramones covering "Needles and Pins," signed The Searchers to a two-album deal. These albums were critically well-received for fitting into the New Wave Pop landscape but were commercial failures, leading Sire to drop the band. "Apparently, during those sessions, Curtis, who had given up music and become a civil servant, would regularly phone the studio threatening to burn it down if he wasn't involved."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Skiffle Group vs. Country/Rock and Roll Group
podcast.body: Mike Pender vehemently denies that he or the group were ever involved in Skiffle, insisting he disliked the genre and that if John McNally had a Skiffle group, it was before Pender joined. Pender claims he and McNally co-formed a group that was "definitely absolutely not in any way a Skiffle group" and was not led by McNally. "According to Pender, he never liked Skiffle, never played Skiffle and if McNally had a Skiffle group it must have been before I met him."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Strong Harmony Vocals
podcast.body: The Searchers were considered the best harmony group in Liverpool outside of The Beatles, and the only other one with multiple strong lead vocalists, with their harmonies inspired more by The Everly Brothers than by soul groups. "Other than the Beatles, the searchers were the best harmony group in Liverpool, and were the only other one to have multiple strong lead vocalists."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Tony Hatch's Pseudonym for "Sugar and Spice"
podcast.body: Tony Hatch used the pseudonym "Fred Nightingale" when presenting "Sugar and Spice" to the group, a common practice for producers at the time to hide their authorship from labels. The group was later angry upon discovering his deception. "In this case, he brought the group a song that he claimed to be missing by one Fred Nightingale, and which he thought would be perfect for them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Tony Jackson's Departure and Disputes
podcast.body: Tony Jackson, who regarded himself as the lead singer, felt sidelined as Mike Pender took over lead vocals on hits. Musical differences (Jackson preferring harder R&B while the group moved melodic) and personality conflicts, including a fistfight with Pender on stage, led to his departure. Jackson claimed he was pushed out so Chris Curtis could bring in his boyfriend (Frank Allen), which Allen denied. "The combination of these musical differences and his feelings about having his place usurped, meant that Jackson was increasingly getting annoyed at the other three band members."
